chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Legal and Regulatory Framework

lessons.title: Cash Components, Circle Rates and Benami Law

children.text: Manish finds a resale flat in Noida Sector 50 for ₹1.5 crore. The seller has one condition: "₹1.2 crore in the registry, ₹30 lakh in cash. You save on stamp duty, I save on tax. Everyone does it." It sounds like a win-win. It is actually one of the most expensive mistakes a buyer can make, and it can break several laws at once. This lesson explains circle rates, why cash components exist, what they really cost you, and how benami law treats property held in someone else's name.

body.text: A cash component does not save you money. It swaps a small, visible stamp duty saving for a lower loan, a bigger tax bill later, no legal proof of what you paid, and exposure to penalties as large as the cash itself.

children.text: Circle Rates: The Government's Floor Price

markDefs.definition: The value of a property calculated using the government's circle rate, ready reckoner rate or guideline value. Stamp duty is charged on this value or the agreement value, whichever is higher.

children.text: As you learned in Chapter 3, each state sets a minimum value per square foot for every locality, called the circle rate, ready reckoner rate or guideline value. Multiply it by a property's area and you get its

. Circle rates are revised only periodically, so they often lag the real market. In prime, fast-rising areas, market prices can sit well above circle rates. In slow markets, circle rates can end up above what buyers will actually pay.

body.title: When circle rates and market prices drift apart

columns.label: Market price above circle rate
points: Creates the temptation to register at the lower circle rate and pay the rest in cash
Stamp duty on the registered value looks lower
The gap is where cash components hide

columns.label: Circle rate above market price
points: Happens in stagnant or falling markets
Buyers must still pay stamp duty on the higher circle rate value
Income tax rules can treat the gap as extra income for the buyer and extra sale value for the seller
Genuine deals can get stuck until circle rates are revised

children.text: How Income Tax Uses the Circle Rate

Income tax law uses the stamp duty value as a check on under-reporting. If a property is registered for less than its stamp duty value, and the gap is larger than the permitted tolerance, two things generally happen. The seller's capital gains are calculated as if the sale happened at the stamp duty value. And the buyer can be taxed on the difference as income, if it exceeds ₹50,000. The permitted tolerance is 10%, and similar rules continue under the Income-tax Act, 2025, which applies from April 2026.

body.latex: \text{Tax adjustment applies if} \quad \text{Stamp Duty Value} > 1.10 \times \text{Registered Sale Price}
body.caption: Within the 10% tolerance, the registered price is generally accepted. Beyond it, both buyer and seller face tax consequences.
Does the 10% tolerance protect the deal?

cells: Beyond tolerance: buyer may be taxed on ₹15 lakh; seller's gains computed on ₹1 crore

body.title: The buyer's tax on the gap
body.prompt: Pooja buys a flat in Jaipur registered at ₹80 lakh. Its stamp duty value is ₹95 lakh. Since ₹95 lakh is more than 110% of ₹80 lakh (₹88 lakh), the gap is taxable as her income. How much is added to her income, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: ₹95 lakh minus ₹80 lakh = ₹15 lakh is added to her income. In the 30% slab plus 4% cess, that is about ₹4.68 lakh of tax. The seller, meanwhile, has capital gains computed as though he sold at ₹95 lakh.

markDefs.definition: The part of a property's price paid in unaccounted cash, outside the registered sale deed.

children.text: exists because both sides think they gain. The seller reports a lower sale price and pays less capital gains tax, and may want to park unaccounted cash. The buyer pays stamp duty on a lower figure. What neither side says out loud is that the cash is unaccounted money, and both parties are now tied into an illegal transaction with no written record.
What Manish's ₹30 Lakh Cash Deal Really Costs

Assume the flat's stamp duty value is ₹1.2 crore, so registering at ₹1.2 crore stays within the rules on paper. Manish pays UP stamp duty at 7%. He plans to take a home loan at the 75% LTV cap and to sell the flat in about 10 years for ₹2.5 crore.

body.title: Manish's cash deal: the saving vs the costs (₹ lakh, illustrative)

data.label: Cash exposed to penalty and loss

body.text: Cash rules make these deals dangerous for both sides. Income tax law generally prohibits accepting ₹20,000 or more in cash as an advance or payment linked to a property transfer, and receiving ₹2 lakh or more in cash in a single transaction. The penalty can equal the entire cash amount. On ₹30 lakh of cash, that is a potential ₹30 lakh penalty, on top of the tax on unexplained money for whoever cannot show where the cash came from.

body.title: Spot the real saving
body.question: A seller offers to register a ₹1 crore flat at ₹80 lakh, with ₹20 lakh paid in cash. Stamp duty is 6%. Which statement is true?
options: The buyer saves ₹6 lakh in stamp duty with no downside
The buyer saves ₹1.2 lakh in stamp duty but gets a smaller loan, a lower recorded cost for future capital gains, no proof of the cash paid, and penalty exposure
The deal is legal if both parties agree in writing
Banks will lend against the full ₹1 crore value
body.explanation: Stamp duty saved is 6% of ₹20 lakh = ₹1.2 lakh. In exchange, the loan is based on ₹80 lakh, future capital gains are computed from a ₹80 lakh cost, the ₹20 lakh has no legal record, and cash rules can trigger penalties. And if the stamp duty value is above ₹80 lakh, stamp duty is charged on that higher value anyway.

children.text: Benami Property: Owning Through Someone Else's Name

markDefs.definition: A transaction where property is held by or transferred to one person, the benamidar, while the money is provided by another person, the beneficial owner, for whose benefit it is held.
The person in whose name a benami property is held, while someone else actually paid for it and benefits from it.

children.text: "Benami" literally means without a name. A
is when someone buys property with their money but puts it in another person's name, the

, often to hide wealth, dodge tax or keep assets away from creditors or investigators. The Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988, significantly strengthened by an amendment that took effect on 1 November 2016, allows authorities to attach and confiscate such property.

body.label: Consequences under the amended benami law
body.value: Confiscation, rigorous imprisonment of 1 to 7 years, and a fine of up to 25% of fair market value
body.context: These are the penalties the 2016 amendment introduced for entering into benami transactions. Constitutional challenges to parts of the law remain before the Supreme Court, but the law remains in force.

body.caption: What is generally not treated as benami

cells: Property bought in the name of a spouse or child
Paid for from the buyer's known sources of income
Property held jointly with a brother, sister, parent or child
The names appear as joint owners, and it is paid from known sources
Property held by a Karta for a Hindu Undivided Family
Held for the benefit of the family, from known sources
Property held in a fiduciary capacity
Such as a trustee, executor or company director acting for others

body.text: The key phrase in every exception is "known sources of income." Buying a flat in your wife's name with salary saved in your bank account is generally fine. Buying a plot in your driver's or a distant cousin's name, paid with cash that appears nowhere in your records, is the textbook benami transaction. And the benamidar faces risk too: the property can be confiscated from them, and they can be prosecuted.

events.title: Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act passed
events.description: Benami transactions are prohibited, but enforcement machinery is weak for decades.

events.title: Amended law takes effect
events.description: A detailed framework for attachment, adjudication, confiscation and prosecution comes into force.

events.title: Ganpati Dealcom judgment
events.description: The Supreme Court holds that the 2016 amendment cannot apply retrospectively and strikes down certain provisions of the original law.

events.title: Judgment recalled
events.description: On review, the Supreme Court recalls the 2022 judgment and sends the matter for fresh hearing before a new bench.

body.title: The government's floor price
body.textWithBlank: In Delhi and Uttar Pradesh, the government's minimum property value per sq m used for stamp duty is called the ___ rate.
body.explanation: Delhi and UP call it the circle rate, Maharashtra calls it the ready reckoner rate, and Karnataka and Tamil Nadu call it the guideline value. All work the same way.

body.title: The plot in the cousin's name
body.scenario: Harish runs a successful trading business in Lucknow. Much of his income is received in cash and not fully reported. His uncle suggests buying a ₹60 lakh plot in the name of Harish's cousin, who lives in a village, and paying ₹40 lakh of it in cash, "so nothing comes back to you."
body.prompt: What legal and financial risks does this plan carry for Harish and his cousin?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Textbook benami: Harish pays, the cousin holds the title, and the money is not from known, disclosed sources. None of the family exceptions apply.
2. Confiscation: authorities can attach and confiscate the plot, so Harish could lose the entire ₹60 lakh.
3. Prosecution and fines: both the beneficial owner and the benamidar can face rigorous imprisonment of 1 to 7 years and a fine of up to 25% of the property's fair market value.
4. Cash violations: ₹40 lakh in cash to the seller breaches cash transaction limits, exposing the seller to a penalty that can equal the cash amount, and inviting scrutiny of where the cash came from.
5. Income tax: unexplained cash used for the purchase can be taxed as unexplained income at high rates, with penalties.
6. Family risk: legally, the plot belongs to the cousin. If the cousin refuses to return it, sells it, dies, or has creditors, Harish has no enforceable claim, because courts will not help enforce an illegal arrangement.
7. The better route: report income properly, pay tax, and buy in his own name or jointly with close family from known sources.

body.title: Keep Your Property Purchase Clean
steps: Look up the circle rate or ready reckoner value before negotiating
Register the sale deed at the actual price agreed
Pay every rupee through banking channels and keep records
Reject any request for a cash component, however it is framed
If buying in a family member's name, fund it from known, documented income
Check whether the registered price is within 10% of the stamp duty value
Ask a tax professional about the tax effect before registering any below-circle-rate deal

body.label: IGRS Uttar Pradesh: Circle Rates and Registration
body.description: Check UP's circle rates and property registration services. Other states publish ready reckoner rates and guideline values on their registration portals.

body.title: Cash, Circle Rate and Benami Terms

cards.definition: A property's value at the government circle rate, used as a floor for stamp duty and as a check in income tax.
Income tax generally accepts a registered price if the stamp duty value is no more than 110% of it.
Unaccounted cash paid outside the registered sale deed. Illegal, unenforceable and penalty-prone.
Property held in one person's name while another pays for and benefits from it.
The person in whose name a benami property is held.
Documented, disclosed income. Buying in a spouse's or child's name from such income is generally not benami.

points: Circle rates set a floor for stamp duty, and income tax uses them as a check, with a 10% tolerance.
Registering below stamp duty value beyond tolerance can tax the buyer on the gap and the seller on the higher value.
In Manish's example, a ₹2.1 lakh stamp duty saving came with ₹22.5 lakh less loan, ₹3.75 lakh extra future tax and no proof of ₹30 lakh paid.
Cash of ₹20,000 or more linked to a property transfer, or ₹2 lakh or more in one transaction, can attract a penalty equal to the amount.
Benami property can be confiscated, with imprisonment of 1 to 7 years and fines of up to 25% of fair market value.
Buying in a spouse's or child's name from known income is generally fine; buying in anyone's name with unaccounted cash is not.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal or tax advice. Tax provisions were renumbered under the Income-tax Act, 2025, and thresholds, penalties and interpretations can change; parts of benami law remain under judicial review. Examples are illustrative. Consult a qualified lawyer and a tax professional before any property transaction.
